Which of the following opposed British in India vigorously?
x: Marathas opposed the British vigorously in India. Maratha were suppressed after three Anglo-Maratha Wars. On the ruins of Mughal Empire, Maratha laid down their foundation and British also took advantage of these circumstances. British lost first Anglo-Maratha war badly and this war ended with the Treaty of Salbai. Lord Wellesley trapped Peshwa in the cage of Subsidiary Alliance in 1802. Lord Hastings established British supremacy after the devastation of remnant strength of Marathas in 1818. Regional States : Punjab and Mysore *Ranjit Singh was born to the chief of Sukerchakia Misl on 13 th November, 1780 A.D. Treaty of Amritsar was signed between Maharaja Ranjit Singh and British East India Company on 25 th April, 1809 A.D. Ranjit Singh captured Multan in 1818 A.D., Kashmir in 1819 and Peshawar and North-West frontier (Khyber-Pakhtunkhwa) in 1834 A.D.. *In 1798 AD, Zaman Shah attacked Punjab. While returning, his cannons accidentally fell into the Jhelam River (some sources refer for Chenab River but Jhelam River is authenticated by many historians). These cannons were sent back to Jaman Shah by Ranjit Singh. Happy with this gesture of Ranjit Singh, Jaman Shah allowed Ranjit Singh to rule Lahore. As a result, in 1799 A.D., Ranjit Singh took control of Lahore and made it his Capital. Zaman Shah gave him the title of Raja (in return of his service and providing tanks and artileries) and appointed him as the Subedar of Lahore. He also captured Amritsar from Bhangi Misl in 1802

Consider the following events of Modern Indian History
1. Death sentence to Raja Nand Kumar
2. Treaty of Salbai
3. Battle of Wandiwash
4. Death of Tipu Sultan Which of the following is the correct chronological order of the above events?
x: The accepted years of these four events are as follows– Battle of Wandiwash (1760) – A decisive battle fought between the British and the French during the Third Carnatic War. This is the earliest among the four. Death sentence awarded to Raja Nandkumar (1775) – Raja Nandkumar, a hindu Brahmin and former landlord of Berhampur, was tried on charges of forgery and hanged at Calcutta. Treaty of Salbai (1782) – The agreement between the East India Company and the Marathas at the end of the First Anglo– Maratha War (1775–1782) is called the Treaty of Salbai. Death of Tipu Sultan (1799) – Tipu Sultan, the ruler of Mysore, was killed during the Battle of Srirangapatnam in the Fourth Anglo–Mysore War (1799).

s: Which statement best explains the historical significance of the Anglo-Maratha Wars?

s: Which one of the following statements is correct regarding British paramountcy in India?

Under the Treaty of Seringapatam (1792), which ended the Third Anglo-Mysore War, Tipu Sultan:
o: was killed and Mysore was partitioned
gave up half his territory, paid Rs 3 crore and sent two sons as hostages
accepted a subsidiary alliance and restored the Wodeyars
returned all conquests under mutual restitution
x: Under the Treaty of Seringapatam, Tipu gave up half his territory, paid Rs 3 crore and handed over two sons as hostages to the British, Marathas and Nizam, who were allied against him. Tipu was killed and Mysore partitioned in 1799, in the Fourth war, when the Wodeyars were restored. Mutual restitution was agreed in the Treaty of Madras of 1769.

s: At a time when empires in Europe were crumbling before the might of Napoleon, which one of the following Governors-General kept the British flag flying high in India?
x: Lord Wellesley (1798–1805) pursued an aggressive forward policy through subsidiary alliances, expanding British control despite Britain's struggle with France. His annexations and diplomacy secured British supremacy in India, earning him credit for "keeping the flag flying" during the Napoleonic era.

s: At a time when empires in Europe were crumbling before the might of Napoleon, which one of the following Governors-General kept the British flag flying high in India?
x: Lord Wellesley moved to India in 1797 A.D., which was the darkest period of British history. The front made of European powers against France had been disbanded. Napoleon had conquered Egypt and Syria and was seriously thinking about attacking India. In that condition, Lord Wellesley used a subsidiary alliance in India, which helped him to establish the sovereignty of the British power and the fear of Napoleon was averted.

s: Subsidiary Alliance was implemented during the reign of –
x: Lord Wellesley (1798-1805) cleverly used a subsidiary alliance as a tool to make Indian provinces puppets of Britishers. He did not discover this method. This method was in practice earlier also but it gradually evolved and the final shape was provided by Wellesley. Dupleix was the first European to give his army to an Indian ruler on the promise of a fixed payment to the Company. Britishers used these tactics too. First Subsidiary Alliance was signed in 1765 with Awadh where Company promised to protect the boundaries of Awadh on a fixed payment to the Company. The evolved version of the Subsidiary Alliance was accepted by the Princely States in the following Sequence- Hyderabad (1798 AD and 1800 AD), Mysore (1799 AD), Tanjore (1799 AD), Oudh (1801 AD), Peshwa (1802), Bhonsle of Barar (1803 AD), Sindhiya (1804 AD), Holkar (1818 AD), Jodhpur, Jaipur, Machheri, Bundi and Bharatpur. Note : Hyderabad will be the answer if it is asked first state to join Wellesley's subsidiary alliance.

s: Who introduced the Subsidiary Alliance System in the administration to establish British power over the Indian States?
x: The doctrine of Subsidiary Alliance System was introduced by Lord Wellesley, British Governor-General of Bengal from 1798-1805. He also adopted a policy of non-intervention in the princely state but later adopted the policy of Subsidiary Alliance. The Nizam of Hyderabad was the first to enter into such an alliance.

s:
Which of the following sites were obtained by the British East India Company under the Treaty of Sugauli in 1816 ?
1. Kathmandu
2. Shimla
3. Ranikhet
4. Nainital
Select the correct answer from the code given below :
x: As a result of the Treaty of Sugauli (1816), Nepal ceded to the British East India Company Kumaon, the eastern part of Garhwal, and some parts of the Terai. The areas included in Kumaon came under British rule. Kathmandu: It remained the capital of Nepal; the treaty only provided for the appointment of a British Resident. Kathmandu was not handed over to the British. Shimla: British control was established over the hill tract in which Shimla is located; however, the actual transfer of land for the “Shimla station/town” took place in 1830 from Keonthal/Patiala. Ranikhet: Ranikhet is located in the Kumaon region (present-day Uttarakhand). After the Treaty of Sugauli, Kumaon came under British control. Nainital: Nainital is also a part of Kumaon; once Kumaon came under British rule, this area too came under Company administration.

s: The Treaty of Yandabu was signed in
x: The Treaty of Yandabo (Yandabu) ended the First Anglo-Burmese War under Amherst and was signed in 1826, not 1824 (when the war began) or 1825.

s: Which British general forced Nepal to accept terms in the Anglo-Nepal War in 1815?

s: Which territories did the British gain by the Treaty of Yandabo (1826)?

s: With which Governor-General is the Tripartite Treaty of 1838 associated?
x: The Tripartite Treaty (1838) preceded the First Anglo-Afghan War under Auckland.

s: Which one of the following was the immediate cause of the First Anglo-Sikh War?
o: The murder of Vans Agnew and Anderson at Multan
The refusal of the Nizam to assign Berar
The Sikh army crossing the Sutlej
The detention of two British doctors in Sikkim

s: What triggered the Second Anglo-Sikh War (1848-49)?
o: the Sikh army crossing the Sutlej
the murder of British officers Vans Agnew and Anderson at Multan
the death of Maharaja Ranjit Singh
the sale of Kashmir to Gulab Singh
x: It began after the British officers Vans Agnew and Anderson were murdered at Multan, under Dalhousie. The Sutlej crossing caused the First war (1845). Ranjit Singh's death in 1839 was the background to both wars. Kashmir went to Gulab Singh in 1846, after the First war.

s:

Securing the trade of the Indus
Introducing the Doctrine of Lapse in Sindh

s: During British rule in India, Indian states had freedom in internal administration but had no international life. But the British interfered in internal administration under the following conditions

On the request of the Congress party
On the request of the people

s: Who among the following negotiated Subordinate Alliances of 1817-18 with the Princely States of Rajputana?

Charles Metcalf was entrusted with the duty of negotiating alliances with princely states of Rajputana.

Which of the following were the social reforms introduced by William Bentinck?
1. Abolition of Sati
2. Abolition of slavery
3. Removal of disabilities due to change of religion
4. Suppression of the organized bands of Thugs.
Choose the correct answer from the codes given below.
x: Lord William Bentinck became the Governor General of Bengal presidency in 1828 A.D. In 1829 A.D., he declared the 'practice of sati' a crime and abolished it. Bentick tried to suppress thugs by running a campaign against the gang of thugs. Bentinck also worked on education and freedom of the press. In the time period of Bentinck, Charter Act, 1833 was passed which abolished slavery. In 1835 he went back to England. The provision of disqualification due to change of religion was removed in 1850 A.D. Hence, statements (1), (2) and (4) are correct, so option (c) will be the answer.
